🌎 BEYOND THE 956

Simon Winchester, the British-American author and journalist whose 1998 bestseller The Professor and the Madman told the extraordinary story behind the making of the Oxford English Dictionary, has died at 82.

Winchester died of a heart attack at his farm in Sandisfield, Massachusetts, on November 3, 2026, according to reports.

Born September 28, 1944, in London, Winchester trained as a geologist before switching to journalism. As a correspondent for The Guardian, he covered some of the defining stories of the twentieth century, including Bloody Sunday in Northern Ireland and the Watergate scandal in Washington.

His breakthrough as an author came in 1998 with The Professor and the Madman — published in Britain as The Surgeon of Crowthorne — the tale of the scholar James Murray and the asylum inmate William Chester Minor, whose unlikely collaboration helped build the Oxford English Dictionary. The book became a New York Times bestseller and was later adapted into a film starring Mel Gibson and Sean Penn.

He followed it with a string of bestselling works of narrative nonfiction, including The Map That Changed the World (2001), Krakatoa: The Day the World Exploded (2003), Atlantic (2010) and Pacific (2015). Across a career spanning more than five decades, he wrote or contributed to more than 30 bestselling books. In 2006, he was made an Officer of the Order of the British Empire for services to journalism and literature.

Rest in Peace, Simon Winchester.

Sources: The New York Times; Wikipedia.
